summary: Defines the protocol IRC servers use to talk to one another, which lets many servers act together as one chat network. It is an informational memo and builds on the IRC architecture document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2813 defines how Internet Relay Chat (IRC) servers exchange information and relay activity across a network. Each server keeps a network-wide database and updates it when servers, users, channels or links change.

questions: how do irc servers talk to each other
what does the irc server command do
how does irc flood control work
subtitle: How IRC servers exchange users, channels and messages across a connected network.

tldr.problem: IRC servers need a common protocol to exchange messages and state so users connected to different servers can participate in one network.
tldr.mechanism: Servers connect as an acyclic network, authenticate and introduce links with PASS and SERVER, and share server, client and channel state in a defined order.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2813 is an Informational memo that updates RFC 1459. It states that requiring every server to know every server, client and channel creates scalability problems.

today: RFC 2813 is an Informational memo that updates RFC 1459. The batch metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes RFC 2813.

sections.title: The Shared Network Database
sections.content:
IRC servers relay messages between clients and host channels. Each server keeps a global state database that is intended to be identical across the network. It records servers, clients and channels known to that server.

Users have network-wide nicknames, and servers keep their host, username and home server information. Services have a nickname and server name, can request some global state and cannot join channels. A server may use a hostmask so servers outside an area see it as one virtual server.
sections.plainLanguage: Every IRC server keeps information about the wider network, not only its own clients. Servers use this shared information to find the correct destination for messages.

sections.title: Server Messages and Origin Checks
sections.content:
Server messages use an optional origin prefix, a command and up to fifteen parameters. A message ends with CR-LF and must not exceed 512 characters including those ending characters. Most server-to-server messages perform routing work and do not generate a reply.

A receiving server checks the prefix against its internal database. If the source is unknown, the message is discarded and the receiving server may have to drop the link. If a message claims to come from a client on the wrong server link, the server issues a KILL; server-link inconsistencies require dropping the link.
sections.plainLanguage: The prefix identifies where a message came from. A server checks that identity before forwarding the message, and discards messages that do not match the network state it knows.

sections.title: Connecting Servers and Introducing Clients
sections.content:
Servers exchange a PASS command before SERVER. PASS includes a connection password and server version; it can also carry options for compression and anti-abuse protections. SERVER introduces a server name, hop count, link-specific token and information string. A duplicate server route must be closed to preserve the acyclic network.

Servers introduce new users to other servers with an extended NICK message that combines nickname, user, mode and server information. SERVICE introduces services. The forms used between servers are distinct from the client registration commands.
sections.plainLanguage: Two servers exchange connection information before becoming peers. They then use server messages to announce the other servers and clients that each side knows.

sections.title: State Exchange, Splits and Flood Control
sections.content:
When servers connect, they exchange state in this order: known servers, known clients, then known channels. Server information comes first so server collisions are detected before nickname collisions. NJOIN efficiently transfers channel membership when links connect.

When a server link closes, the detecting server informs the rest of the network with SQUIT messages for the servers behind that link. Servers also keep nickname history and may delay reuse of nicknames after a split or KILL. Flood control applies a two-second penalty per client message within a ten-second window; the RFC describes this as allowing about one message every two seconds without adverse effect.
sections.plainLanguage: When two server groups connect, they first exchange server lists, then client details and channel membership. When a link fails, servers announce which part of the network is no longer connected.

sections.title: Scalability and Security Limits
sections.content:
The RFC says the protocol does not scale well because every server must know about all servers, clients and channels and update that information when it changes. Names can collide, and servers do few consistency checks on information received from neighboring servers.

Server authentication relies on plaintext passwords and DNS lookups, which the RFC describes as weak and unsafe. PASS and OPER messages are sent in clear text; the memo notes that a stream-encryption layer such as TLS could protect those transactions.
sections.plainLanguage: The network-wide database becomes harder to maintain as the IRC network grows. The memo also warns that its password and DNS-based authentication is weak, and points to stream encryption as a way to protect credentials.
